t: The Aoun (Awn) Family, from Damour to Brooklyn
x: What we found The family was Aoun in Damour. The family says the name became Awn in America ( Family ), and records also wrote it Owen and Aun; Joseph’s death certificate says Owen ( Confirmed ). The Awn story begins in Damour, a coastal village south of Beirut. Damour sits on the Mediterranean coast about eleven miles south of Beirut. When the Aouns left in the summer of 1920, the First World War had only just ended, and Mount Lebanon was recovering from a wartime famine that, by most historians' estimates, killed a large share of its people. In September 1920, as the family crossed into New York State, France was proclaiming the new state of Greater Lebanon under its mandate. This is background, not a record of this family, and the papers do not tell us why Joseph and Assin decided to go. What they do tell us is that they took all eight children with them, a party of ten on third-class tickets by way of Southampton and Quebec, with Joseph about 50 years old and an uncle waiting in Brooklyn. That is a lot to stake on a new country.

What we found Joseph’s death certificate says “Joseph K. Owen,” but the Arabic papers call him Joseph Khoury, son of Boutros, so the K. stands for Khoury ( Confirmed ). Leaving Damour with eight children In the summer of 1920, Joseph Aoun was about fifty. He took his wife Assin and eight children aboard on third-class tickets, by way of Southampton and Quebec, bound for an uncle, Michal Malleut, who was waiting in Brooklyn. The youngest, Anthony, was six. He would become our grandfather ( Confirmed : the 1920 ship manifest). Family memory: why they left, or what the trip was like. If you know, please tell me. They settled in Brooklyn. By 1932 Joseph was retired. Between them Joseph and Assin buried a son, Nassib, in 1924, and another, George, in 1930. They had also left a daughter, Esther, behind in Lebanon ( Confirmed : death certificates and the Arabic death notices of 1930 and 1935). Joseph died on 14 September 1932. Assin died on 16 October 1935 at Bay Ridge Hospital, and her son John signed for the burial permit ( Confirmed ). 1869 Joseph is born 1920 Ten people cross the ocean together 1924 and 1930 Nassib and George die 1932 and 1935 Joseph dies, then Assin The details: spellings, certificates and what the Arabic papers add Anthony's father, Joseph Aoun , was born 21 November 1869 and died in Brooklyn at about 1 a.m. on 14 September 1932, aged 62. His death certificate spells the family name Owen, lists him as retired, and gives his parents as Peter and Teresa. The cause was cardiac failure from a coronary thrombosis, and he was buried at St. John's Cemetery on 16 September ( Confirmed , NYC death certificate no. 18405). On the 1920 ship manifest he is Youseuf Aoun, a farmer or traveler of 53. The certificate says he had lived in the U.S. for 12 years, which fits the 1920 arrival. The documents behind this 4 documents Document 82 Joseph's death certificate (14 September 1932) Document 83 Assin's death certificate (16 October 1935) Document 133 Joseph's death notice, September 1932 Document 134 Assin's death notice, October 1935 His wife Assin Aoun (written Essine on the manifest and Aseen in the 1925 census) was the daughter of Joseph Segan (Segen; Sajaan in Arabic) and Susanne, whose family name reads Nahmir on the certificate ( Probable ). She died on Wednesday 16 October 1935 at Bay Ridge Hospital, a widow living at 1047 75th Street, of a ruptured appendix after an emergency appendectomy (Al-Hoda also says appendicitis). The Arabic notices call her a woman from Damour. A Mass was said for her at Our Lady of Lebanon on Friday 18 October, the day she was buried at St. John’s, and her son John signed for the burial permit ( Confirmed : certificate; Mira’at al-Gharb, 18 October, and Al-Hoda, 16 to 19 October 1935; one line in Al-Hoda names St. Joseph’s church instead). Her age is written four different ways across the records (45, 40, 50 and 52), so her birth year is unknown. Her death record also spells the name Owen ( Confirmed ). The same undertaker, Jere J. Cronin, Inc., on Atlantic Avenue, handled the funerals of Joseph, Assin and their son Nassib. Assin’s notice also names a circle of close relatives: the sons of Habib Aoun (Sajaan, Khaleel, Farid, Sa’id and Shaker) and the Aql family. Exactly how they were related to Joseph or Assin is not yet known ( Probable as kin only). Joseph lies in St. John’s Cemetery, Section 3, Row C, Grave 4A, while Assin and her son George share Section 20, Row S, Grave 207; why they are apart is not known (Find a Grave). The Arabic-language newspapers of the day add what the certificates leave out. (Our English readings of these notices are our own translations and still need a native Arabic reader to confirm.) They write Joseph’s name as Joseph Khoury, son of Boutros (Peter), so the K. on his death certificate stands for Khoury, and they say he was from Damour ( Confirmed ). They report that he died on the morning of Wednesday 14 September 1932 of a heart attack, with the Mass on Friday 16 September ( Confirmed : Al-Hoda, 14 to 17 September 1932). Where the funeral was held is not settled: the Brooklyn Times Union (item 133) says St. Mary’s Syrian Roman Catholic Church, while the Arabic papers say Our Lady of Lebanon. Joseph had two brothers: Michel, who stayed in Damour, and Gabriel, who died in Brazil in about early 1926 ( Confirmed : Ash-Shams, 1 March 1926). Questions for the family Does anyone know why Assin and George lie apart from Joseph at St. John’s? Does anyone remember Esther, or a letter from Lebanon? Who were the sons of Habib Aoun named in Assin’s notice?

What we found The 1920 ship list shows eight children, but the Arabic death notices of 1930 and 1935 name a ninth, Esther, who stayed in Lebanon ( Confirmed ). Eight on the ship, one who stayed Joseph and Assin had nine children. Eight crossed together in 1920, from Nassib, the oldest, to Anthony, the youngest on the ship. The ninth, Esther, stayed in Lebanon, married there, and died in Beirut in 1961 ( Confirmed : the 1920 manifest, the Arabic death notices of 1930 and 1935, and a 1961 Caravan notice). Two of the brothers died young. Nassib died on 2 October 1924 of pneumonia and tuberculosis, and George drowned in a boat accident on 27 July 1930 ( Confirmed : his death certificate and the Arabic papers). Family stories say one brother drowned and another died after surgery on his arm; the records bear out the drowning, but not the surgery ( Family ). His funeral was on Wednesday 30 July at 2 p.m. at Our Lady of Lebanon, 295 Hicks Street, and he was buried at St. John’s Cemetery, Section 20, Row S, Grave 207 ( Confirmed : Mira’at al-Gharb, 28 to 30 July; Al-Hoda, 29 and 30 July; As-Sayeh, 31 July 1930; Find a Grave memorial 168999663). Two things are still open. The papers do not agree on where it happened: the New York papers point to Long Island, and one Arabic paper (Ash-Shams, September 1930) says a lake in Rhode Island, so we say only that he drowned. And his age is 24 in the notices, 21 in the census and 22 in Ash-Shams. One notice may suggest he was engaged to be married; that is only Possible, and we would like to know more. He is not named in his parents’ 1932 and 1935 notices, which makes sense: he had died before either. Elias (Louis) (born 3 May 1912). Louis is the name the 1930 census, his 1937 marriage certificate and the newspaper notices use; the Arabic notices give both names for the same man ( Confirmed ). Family stories (told by Aunt Jackie) say that two of Anthony’s brothers died young: one drowned, and one died of peritonitis after surgery on his arm. The records now bear out the first half. George drowned in July 1930, and Nassib died in October 1924 ( Confirmed ). Nassib’s certificate gives pneumonia and tuberculosis, not surgery, so the story of the arm surgery does not match either brother yet. It may be a memory that has blended with another family illness, and it is still an open question. Questions for the family Does anyone know Esther’s birth year, or the names of her grandchildren? Who was the brother who, in the family story, died after surgery on his arm? Does anyone know who “Mrs. Mary Awn” of Beirut was?

Ten people, one ship On 25 August 1920 the Aoun family left Southampton on the S.S. Grampian, bound for Quebec. They went on by train and crossed into New York State at Rouses Point on 5 September 1920 ( Confirmed : the ship’s manifest, Anthony’s immigration card and his own petition). The manifest lists the household together, heading for the uncle, Michal Malleut, in Brooklyn, with Damour as their last home. Joseph is written Youseuf, 53, and Assin Essine, 45. Ship ages are approximate: Anthony is 4 on the manifest, but 6 by his birth date ( Confirmed : names; Family : that all eight are brothers and sisters). 25 Aug 1920 Leave Southampton 5 Sep 1920 Cross into New York State at Rouses Point Then On to Brooklyn The details: records, spellings and open questions In the summer of 1920 the Aoun party left Southampton on the S.S. Grampian on 25 August, bound for Quebec, and crossed into New York State at Rouses Point on 5 September 1920 ( Confirmed : the manifest, Anthony's immigration ID card, and his own petition, which says he entered as Antoine Aoun by the Delaware & Hudson Railway). A house full of working children By 1925 the family lived at 37 Tompkins Place in Brooklyn. The state census that year lists nine people at home, all born in Syria: Joseph, Assin and seven of their children. Nassib was missing, because he had died there the October before ( Confirmed : 1925 state census). By April 1930 Mathilde had married and moved out. John was a manager in a dry goods business, Theresa a clerk in dry goods, George a manager in ladies’ apparel and Mitchell a clerk ( Confirmed : 1930 census). The family says only Anthony and Mitchell were allowed to go to school while the others worked ( Family ). Four brothers, one path The four brothers who settled in New York each became citizens between 1941 and 1943, and each followed the same steps: a declaration of intention, a petition, and an oath taken with two witnesses ( Confirmed : their naturalization papers). Mathilde took her oath on 30 June 1942. Theresa waited until 10 May 1955. Mitchell’s papers include a court order of 9 June 1943 that made Awn his legal name ( Confirmed ). Friends from Clinton Street, among them Said Owen, a shoemaker, stood as witnesses for several of the brothers. 6 Feb 1941 Elias becomes a citizen 30 Jun 1942 Mathilde becomes a citizen 5 Nov 1942 John becomes a citizen 10 Nov 1942 Anthony becomes a citizen 9 Jun 1943 Mitchell’s name is changed to Awn The details: records, spellings and open questions The brothers each took the same path to citizenship, and the papers survive: Elias : declaration of intention 1937; petition and oath with witnesses 1941. Mitchell : declaration 1939; WWII draft card 1940; petition; and a name-change order in 1943. John : declaration 1940; petition and oath with witnesses 1942. Anthony : declaration 1939; draft card 1940; petition and oath on 10 November 1942. See Part Three. Questions for the family Does anyone have a citizenship certificate or a photograph from one of these ceremonies? Does anyone remember the brothers talking about taking the oath?

t: The brothers' and sisters' later lives
x: Five lives within a few blocks The brothers and sisters who stayed in the New York area made their homes close together, first in Bay Ridge and on Clinton Street, and later on 86th Street. Awn’s Specialty Shop at 82 Greenwich Street ties three of the brothers together: John owned it in 1940, Mitchell worked for him there, and Elias later became a partner ( Confirmed : draft cards, the 1940 census and the New York Times). Mathilde married Fred Gorayeb in 1926 and had no children. Theresa married Michael Koury in 1939 and had three children. John died in 1977, Mitchell in 1978 and Elias in 2001 ( Confirmed : certificates, notices and grave records). John’s birth date is still an open question: a federal court was asked to change it in 1940. 25 Apr 1926 Mathilde marries Fred Gorayeb 18 Apr 1937 Elias marries Isabel 12 Jan 1939 Theresa marries Michael Koury 14 Oct 1940 Mitchell marries Barbara Machanskis 1977 to 2001 John, Mitchell and Elias die The details: records, spellings and open questions John J. Awn (Jean on the manifest, and John Joseph Owen when he signed his name) was the oldest son in the household after Nassib’s death. He first filed to become a citizen in 1926, filed again in 1940 as a merchant living at 1047 75th Street, and took the oath on 5 November 1942 , with Said Owen, a shoemaker, and his brother-in-law Fred Gorayeb as witnesses ( Confirmed , naturalization papers). His birth date puzzled even the courts. In December 1940 the Brooklyn Eagle reported that he asked a federal court to change it from 15 August 1905 to 15 August 1903, and that the Assistant U.S. Attorney opposed the change as an attempt to avoid the draft. Later papers use 4 August 1903, which also fits his ages in the 1925 and 1930 censuses. t: The Saydah Family, from Forzul to Brooklyn
x: Helen's father, Antoon (W.) Saydah , came from Forzul , Lebanon. We call him Antoon, which is how the Arabic papers and his 1942 draft card write his first name; many records write it Anton, and some Antoun. His family name appears as Saydah, Saidah, Sayda, Saida and even Smyda. Helen's mother was born a Hadad (Wassela Hadad), a name that records also spell Hodod, Haddad and Hadel.

A young man from Forzul Antoon Saydah was born in Forzul on 15 August, in 1880 or 1881. By his own sworn word, he left Le Havre on the liner La Touraine in October 1898 and reached New York on 25 October, still in his teens ( Confirmed : his 1909 declaration and 1913 petition, as his own statement). Family memory: stories of the voyage or why he left. If you know, please tell me. The 1900 census finds him in Negaunee, Michigan, a boarder with the Kirkish family, probably his sister Sada’s ( Probable ), selling goods from house to house. By 1910 he was back in Brooklyn, a single man of 29 living with his brother Khaleel and working in embroidered shirtwaists ( Confirmed : census). 1880 or 1881 Antoon is born in Forzul 1898 He arrives in New York 1900 Selling goods in Negaunee, Michigan 1910 Back in Brooklyn, with Khaleel The details: records, spellings and open questions Antoon was born on 15 August 1880 or 1881 (the day is the same in every record, but the year is not) in Forzul. His own sworn 1909 declaration and 1913 petition both say 1881, written "Forgul" in the petition ( Confirmed as his statement). His 1942 draft card gives his parents as Wahbeh Saydah and Noor, whose maiden name is written Kereisati on one record and Jureisaty on his brother's death certificate. The "W." in the three brothers' names stands for their father, Wahbeh ( Confirmed ). A young man of the right name and age, written "Antoun Smyda," 18, appears on a manifest of the French liner La Touraine dated 28 November 1898, going to a brother at 73 Washington Street (sheet 183 of the manifest). This is only Possible, not proven. The manifest's spellings are rough, and Antoon's own sworn papers give a different date: his 1909 declaration and 1913 petition both say he sailed from Le Havre on La Touraine about 17 October and arrived in New York on 25 October 1898, a month earlier ( Confirmed as his own statement). Either the manifest is a different voyage or one of the dates is off, so we still need his name on the 25 October sailing. If the manifest is his, the brother could be Khaleel, who by his own 1910 census and his 1948 biography had arrived in 1891 (other records say 1888 or about 1901). Michael was in Illinois by then, which leaves Khaleel as the only brother we know of in New York (Possible). By April 1910 he was back in Brooklyn at 570 48th Street, living in his brother Khaleel's household as a single man of 29, working as an employee in embroidered shirtwaists ( Confirmed , census), which proves the two were brothers. What we found Wassela’s family name is Hodod on her marriage certificate, Hadad in the 1900 census and Hadel in 1910. It is the same family ( Confirmed ). Engaged a year before the wedding The engagement of Antoon and Wassela Hadad was announced in the Arabic papers on 1 March 1911, more than a year before they married. x: What we found Hanna Hadad died in upstate New York, yet he lies in a grave with no marker in Syracuse, and we do not yet know why ( Probable : Find a Grave). The Hadads of Zahle Wassela’s father, Hanna (John) Hadad, and her mother, Amina Shehadi, were both in America by 1892, according to the census. In 1900 the family was living on DeGraw Street in Brooklyn, in the household of Amina’s probable brother Beshara Shahady ( Confirmed : census; Probable for the brother). Wassela’s brothers Salim, Charles and Najib appear in the censuses. On New Year’s night 1913 a Salim Hadad was shot in the shoulder after a quarrel and sent home. The event is Confirmed ; that he is Wassela’s brother is Probable . That autumn Hanna, who had spent his last eight months at the Clifton Springs health resort, died on 11 October 1913 (where he died is an open conflict, see below), and the funeral was in Syracuse ( Confirmed : Syracuse Post-Standard). 1892 Both parents are in America 1900 DeGraw Street, Brooklyn 1913 Salim is shot, and Hanna dies The details: records, spellings and open questions The family name also appears as Hadad on Wassela’s daughter Evelyn’s Social Security record. Her mother’s maiden name, Shehadi , is also written Shahady. Her parents. Her father appears as John Hodod on her marriage certificate, but the Arabic papers, including the 1912 wedding notice, call him Hanna Haddad (Hanna is the Arabic form of John) and place his home at Mu’allaqa, Zahle ( Confirmed ). Her mother, Amina (Shehadi was her family name), appears as Emmel in 1900 and Ameeny in 1910. For the last eight months of his life Hanna was at the Clifton Springs health resort in upstate New York. He died there on Saturday 11 October 1913, at about 68 (the notices say 68, the 1910 census 65, Find a Grave 66 or 67). The day is Confirmed by two sources, the Syracuse Post-Standard of 13 October 1913 and Find a Grave. Where he died is an open conflict: the Arabic notices and the Post-Standard say Clifton Springs, but the state’s death index lists the entry (certificate no. 50442) under “Willard.” The funeral was held on 13 October at the Church of the Savior, an Episcopal church in Syracuse, and he was buried in Oakwood Cemetery there, in Section H-2, plot 87, in a grave with no marker ( Probable , strong: Find a Grave memorial 115947080). A crash on the road to Brooklyn On Tuesday 5 September 1916 Antoon’s automobile crashed into a fence near Tuxedo Park, New York, on the way back to Brooklyn from Pennsylvania. His friend Najib S. Maloof, riding as his guest, was thrown out and killed instantly ( Confirmed : Arabic papers of 5 and 6 September 1916). The papers do not agree on who was driving: the Arabic papers say Antoon’s brother Khaleel, and the Brooklyn Eagle later said Antoon. Maloof’s widow, Affie, sued Antoon. A jury awarded her $17,500 in June 1918, and the Appellate Division ordered a new trial that December. We have not found how the retrial ended ( Confirmed : as reported in the Eagle; we have not seen the court file). 5 Sep 1916 The crash near Tuxedo Park 24 Jun 1918 Jury awards $17,500 14 Dec 1918 New trial ordered 20 Jan 1919 Case back on the calendar The details: records, spellings and open questions One hard chapter in Antoon’s life reached the newspapers. On Tuesday 5 September 1916 his automobile crashed into a fence near Tuxedo Park, New York, on a trip from Pennsylvania back to Brooklyn. His friend Najib S. Maloof , who was riding as his guest, was thrown out and killed instantly ( Confirmed : Mira’at al-Gharb, 5 and 6 September 1916, p. 3; Al-Hoda, 6 September 1916, p. 3). The papers do not agree on who was driving. The Arabic papers say Antoon’s brother Khaleel was at the wheel of Antoon’s car, while the Brooklyn Eagle later said Antoon was ( Confirmed as printed in each; unresolved). The widow, Affie N. Maloof , sued. The case was on the Kings County Supreme Court calendar by August 1917 (Eagle, 5 August 1917, p. 11), and on 24 June 1918 a jury before Justice Cropsey awarded her $17,500 against Antoon, whom the Eagle called an importer and Maloof’s lifelong friend. That was not the end of it. The Appellate Division reversed the verdict and ordered a new trial (Eagle, 14 December 1918, p. 7, item 144); a request for reargument was denied (11 January 1919, p. 16, item 145), and the case was back on the court calendar on 20 January 1919. We have not found how the retrial ended ( Confirmed as reported; we have not seen the court file). A Najib S. Maloof appears on the 1909 officer list of Damascus Lodge, the Masonic lodge Antoon's brother Khaleel helped found, so the two men probably knew each other through the lodge and the Syrian community ( Probable ). The 1915 Brooklyn tax list assesses Antoon at $60,000 in personal property ( Probable ), which fits an importer doing well. His 1918 draft card gives his business address as 85 Washington Street. We have not yet found Maloof's death record. A teacher who became a merchant Khaleel was the oldest of the brothers we know. As-Sameer printed a short biography of him after his death in 1948. It says he was born in Forzul, studied at the Syrian Protestant College in Beirut, graduating in 1887, and taught at the American school in Sidon and at a school in Zahle before he emigrated in 1891 ( Confirmed as printed; our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader). In America he studied at the Presbyterian seminary in Chicago, left the ministry for business, and became a respected New York merchant. He was an officer of Damascus Lodge when it was founded in 1909, was a witness at Antoon’s wedding in 1912, and put his name to the firm K. W. Saydah & Bros. on Fifth Avenue ( Confirmed : Arabic newspaper advertisements, 1924 to 1925). His death certificate gives his birth as 19 March 1870, while the 1910 census (age 43) points to about 1867. The brother who went west Michael left Lebanon in October 1891 as a teenager and went to Illinois, where he lived in Chicago and Oak Park. He became a citizen on 18 March 1903 in Cook County ( Confirmed : his passport applications; his 1918 draft card gives his birth as 6 August 1877, but that year is open). His 1918 draft card gives his birth as 6 August 1877 in Forzul, though his sons' records suggest about 1870, so the year is open (Uncertain). He left Lebanon in October 1891 as a teenager and went west to Illinois, where he lived in Chicago and Oak Park. That is why he was not the brother waiting in New York in 1898. Two sisters, two Kirkish families Antoon’s sisters Sada and Nustas both married into the Kirkish families, and both were alive when Antoon died in 1949 and Michael in 1953. Awn was born on 6 March 1914 in Damour and arrived at six as Antoine Aoun. He filed his declaration of intention in 1939 and registered for the draft on 16 October 1940. The draft card names his employer as Koury-Awn, Inc. , at 38 East 32nd Street, and gives his brother John at 1047 Bay Ridge Parkway as the person to contact. It also gives his country of citizenship as "France," which probably reflects Lebanon's status under the French Mandate ( Confirmed for the entry; Probable for the reason). His address on the card was changed by hand to a Marine Avenue number in Bay Ridge. We do not know who owned Koury-Awn, Inc. It may have been a business of Anthony's brother-in-law, Michael Koury, who married Theresa in 1939, but that is only a guess (Possible). It may also simply carry the family's own double name, since Mitchell's and Elias's full names were Mitchell and Elias Joseph Khoury Aoun. Mitchell's draft card, written the same day, names a different employer, his brother John at 82 Greenwich Street, so the East 32nd Street firm and the Greenwich Street shop were separate businesses in 1940. He took the oath of citizenship on 10 November 1942 . His petition describes him as 5 feet 8½ inches tall and 172 pounds, living at 123 Marine Avenue, with a wife, Helen (born 9 January 1917 in Brooklyn), a son, Joseph (born 14 November 1941), and a request to be known as Anthony Awn. His two witnesses, Louis Glayat, a salesman on Clinton Street, and Jerome Kinberg, a salesman on West 103rd Street, each swore they had known him since 1 January 1933 ( Confirmed , naturalization papers, spelling used: Awn). The papers give us a picture of him. When he filed his declaration of intention on 4 May 1939, at 25, he was single with no children, living at 1047 Bay Ridge Parkway, and gave his occupation as "negligee salesman." He described himself as dark-complexioned, with brown eyes and dark brown hair, weighing 155 pounds, and gave his race and nationality as Syrian. He said he had entered the United States at Rouses Point, New York, on 5 September 1920 as Antoine Aoun, coming from Quebec on the Delaware & Hudson Railway, and he signed it "Anthony Aoun" ( Confirmed , declaration of intention, spelling used: Aoun). His draft card of 16 October 1940 adds that he was 5 feet 8½ inches and 168 pounds, with light brown hair and a light brown complexion, and an appendicitis scar as his identifying mark ( Confirmed ). Part of good research is knowing which records are not ours. These are written down so nobody has to search for them twice. Joseph Owen, who died 27 April 1932 at 385 Clinton Street, is not Anthony's father. He was a grocer of 55 whose wife was Sadie and whose parents were Michael and Mary, and he had been in the U.S. about 18 years. Our Joseph died in September 1932, aged 62, married to Assin, with parents Peter and Teresa, and had arrived in 1920. The same cemetery (St. John's) and the same undertaker (Jere J. Cronin, Inc.) buried both, but Owen was a common spelling among Brooklyn Syrian families and nothing ties the two men together (Certain: a different man). A "John Khouri" fruit-store lead is not John Awn ( Family , from Sarah). A 1906 petition by a Salim Haddad (born 1883, in the U.S. since 1900, living on Washington Street in Manhattan) and a 1897 Kansas City card for a Salim Hadad are Probably different men from Wassela's brother Salim, who was in Brooklyn by 1892 and in the June 1900 census. The January 1898 ship card for ten-year-old "Wassilah Hadad" Probably describes a different girl, because the Hadads were already living in Brooklyn. The 1920 Ishpeming census page for an Assad Kirkish household (pictured in item 106) is Possible at best. Probably a different Kirkish family, but Assad's wife Sadie could be the "Sada Kirkish" named in the 1953 Eagle notice, so it stays open. George Abraham Saydah of Bay Ridge (1880 to 1963) is not shown to be related. His 1923 declaration and 1926 petition (no. 68097) say he came from Cairo on the Prinzess Irene in August 1906 and lived on Ovington Avenue, with wife Melia and three children born in Hoboken. Nothing in the papers names Antoon, Khaleel or Michael, so he stays here until a record links him (Possible at best; FamilySearch, Brooklyn naturalizations, NARA image group 007784999, images 703, 705 and 706 of 1018, arks 3:1:3Q9M-CSMR-HQP4-4, -HQ2J-P and -HQP4-8). Antone Saddy, a 22-year-old Syrian lodger in the 1920 Manhattan census (sheet 10A, enumeration district 1421; FamilySearch ark 3:1:33SQ-GRNV-WRQ, image 1127 of 1176) is Probably a different man, since Antoon Saydah was in Brooklyn with his wife and daughter in January 1920. “Ambassador George Hakim,” Lebanon’s representative to the United Nations, on the front page of The Caravan, 22 June 1961, is Probably not our George Michael Hakim, the husband of Virginia. Our George was a Brooklyn man, a Columbia graduate and an Army staff sergeant in 1945, and later a marketing executive in New Jersey. Nothing on the page mentions Brooklyn or the Saydah or Awn families, and Hakim is a common Lebanese name (Brooklyn Newsstand, Caravan, 22 June 1961, page 1).

A family history is never finished. These are the open questions. If you know anything about any of them, please use the sharing form below. Anthony and Helen’s wedding. The date, Sunday 29 December 1940, is settled by two Arabic papers and Anthony’s petition. We would still like the marriage certificate, and the name of the church, which is hard to read in the newspaper scan. George Awn. He drowned on 27 July 1930. We do not know where (Long Island or a lake in Rhode Island), why his age is given as 24, 22 and 21, or who the friend with him was. A death record or the New York papers of 28 and 29 July 1930 would settle it. Anthony’s death certificate and Wassela’s 1969 death record. We have Anthony’s death notice (Home Reporter, 15 July 1966) but not his certificate. For Wassela there is a newspaper index entry (The Record of Hackensack, 8 January 1969) and a sympathy notice, but not the certificate. Birth years. Was Antoon born in 1880 or 1881? And when was Wassela born? The 1900 census says 1886, while every later record says about 1889 to 1893. Is Zahleh really her birthplace? A second record for each would settle it. The church. Anthony’s side was Maronite, at Our Lady of Lebanon. The notices say the bride was not Maronite, and the Saydahs used Presbyterian and Episcopal churches (Khaleel studied at a Presbyterian seminary, and Antoon’s funeral was at Christ Episcopal), so they look Protestant ( Probable ). Our Lady of Lebanon’s registers may say more. Lebanon. We have not yet found records from Damour or Forzul. Parish and civil registers there could take us back past Joseph and Antoon. Koury-Awn, Inc., at 38 East 32nd Street, was Anthony's employer in 1940. We would like to know who ran it, and whether Michael Koury (Theresa's husband) was in the clothing business. Esther Ayoub's family in Beirut. The 1961 Caravan notice names her son Antoine Ayoub (with his wife and children) and her daughters Mrs. Sira San Remi and Mrs. Mary Awn of Beirut. It does not name a husband. Does anyone remember them? The Tuxedo Park accident, 1916. Who was driving, Antoon or Khaleel? And how did the new trial of 1919 end? We would like Najib Maloof’s death record and the court file. 73 Washington Street, 1898. The La Touraine entry for "Antoun Smyda" (if it is Antoon) says he was joining a brother at 73 Washington Street. That brother is Probably Khaleel, but we have not shown where Khaleel lived in 1898. A grocer named John Haddad is listed at 73 Washington Street in an 1898 directory, which is Possibly Wassela's father. Did the two families share the address? Antoon's ship and arrival date. He swore he arrived on La Touraine on 25 October 1898. The only matching entry we found, "Antoun Smyda," 18, is on a La Touraine list dated 28 November 1898, and it may not be him. The year 1898 is supported by the 1900 and 1910 censuses, but his own name has not turned up on the 25 October sailing. We need that page, or a record that confirms or rules out the Smyda entry. More open conflicts. Where Hanna Hadad died (Clifton Springs or “Willard”), where Antoon died (Allendale or Columbia, South Carolina), which church held Joseph’s funeral (St. Mary’s or Our Lady of Lebanon), where Sa’da Kirkish lived and who her husband was, and who the Najeeb Hadad of 4721 Sixth Avenue (died 13 January 1914) was. Fred Gorayeb's death, and where he and Mathilde are buried. Mathilde Probably died in December 1984, from an index entry. We have found nothing on Fred's death. Sada and Nustas Kirkish. The 1948, 1949 and 1953 notices for Khaleel, Antoon and Michael all name them as sisters. Sada is Probably "Sady," wife of Abdalla Kirkish, in whose Michigan household Antoon boarded in 1900. We have not yet found a record naming their parents. Michigan death certificates and the Kirkish censuses might. Evelyn and Virginia in 1940. The 1940 census page we found lists only Antoon, Wassela and Helen, and the next sheet has not been checked. The sisters' marriages are known from newspapers and indexes (Virginia in 1945, Evelyn in 1954 and 1971), but we have not seen the marriage certificates. Michael Saydah. Antoon's brother Michael lived in Chicago from about 1891 and moved to Brooklyn around 1916 to 1918 ( Confirmed , from his passport applications and 1918 draft card). He Probably died on 1 March 1953 and was buried in Green-Wood Cemetery on 4 March. We do not know what became of his first wife, Marie Luckey (married in Grundy County, Illinois, in 1901), or whether he was born in 1877, as his own records say, or about 1870, as his sons' certificates imply. His 1903 naturalization papers (Cook County) may name his parents. Mitchell Awn's two wives, Barbara Machanskis and Laurdes Nassr, and what became of Barbara. Living memories. A conversation with family would fill in what no record keeps, such as Esther Ayoub's family and which brother had the arm surgery.

Where the records come from: FamilySearch : census, naturalization and marriage indexes Brooklyn Newsstand : Brooklyn Eagle notices NYC Historical Vital Records : birth, marriage and death certificates NYC Marriage Index Green-Wood Cemetery burial search Find a Grave The New York Times archive and Ancestry Library Edition (in a library) Ellis Island and Quebec border-crossing records Arabic-language newspapers (Al-Hoda, Mira’at al-Gharb, As-Sayeh, Ash-Shams, As-Sameer) through the Khayrallah Center’s Arabic Newspaper Database . Joseph's death certificate, 14 September 1932. The New York City certificate for "Joseph K. Owen," died at about 1 a.m. on 14 September 1932 in Brooklyn, born 21 November 1869, aged 62 years, 9 months, 7 days. It lists him as married to "Assin Owen," retired, 12 years in the U.S. and in New York City, son of "Peter Owen" and "Teresa Owen," both of Syria. The cause is cardiac failure (one day), with coronary thrombosis (six months) contributing, signed by the attending physician. Burial was at St. John's Cemetery on 16 September, with Jere J. Cronin, Inc., of 115 Atlantic Avenue as undertaker. The second picture is the bottom of the back of the certificate, where the undertaker's statement is signed "Mrs. Assin Owen" as the "Wife" of the deceased, the person who asked for the burial permit. ( Confirmed as written; the first name here is Joseph and the family name is spelled Owen.) Source: New York City Department of Health, Standard Certificate of Death, Brooklyn, registered no. 18405 (1932), as viewed on FamilySearch / New York City Municipal Deaths. Name as written: Joseph K. Owen.

Assin's death certificate, 16 October 1935. The certificate for "Assin Owen," a widow aged 52 who did housework, died about 1 a.m. on 16 October 1935 at Bay Ridge Hospital, Brooklyn; she lived at 1047 75th Street and had been in the U.S. and New York City for 14 years. Her father is written "Joseph Segen" (her son Louis's 1937 marriage certificate gives "Segan") and her mother's maiden name appears to read "Susanne Nahmir" (hard to read: the first letter could also be K or H, and the last letter r or e; Probable ). Her date of birth is blank. The cause is acute gangrenous appendicitis (ruptured), after an appendectomy, with toxic myocarditis contributing. She was buried at St. John's Cemetery on 18 October. The back carries the undertaker's statement, which names "John Owen" of 1047 75th Street as her "Son," the next of kin who asked for the burial permit. ( Confirmed as written; the spelling is Owen.) Source: New York City Department of Health, Standard Certificate of Death, Brooklyn, registered no. 20730 (1935), as viewed on FamilySearch / New York City Municipal Deaths. Name as written: Assin Owen.

Joseph's death notice, September 1932. Confirmed as printed: Joseph K. Owen, 62, of 590 78th Street, died "yesterday" at home. He was born in Damour, Syria, and had lived in Brooklyn for 12 years. He leaves his wife, Affin (Assin); four sons, John, Mitchell, Louis and Anthony; and two daughters, Matilda and Theresa. The funeral was to go from the home to St. Mary's Syrian R. C. Church on Hicks Street for a requiem mass, with burial at St. John's Cemetery under J. J. Cronin. Four things stand out. Louis is Elias, who signed his 1937 marriage certificate as Louis J. Awn ( Confirmed ). The same four sons are named in Esther Ayoub’s 1961 notice. George, who was 21 in the April 1930 census, is named in none of the three notices, and neither is Nassib (Nessil), who died in 1924; we now know why. George drowned in July 1930 ( Confirmed , from the Arabic papers of that week) and Nassib died in 1924. The address, 590 78th Street, is not one we have seen elsewhere for the family. And the funeral church is St. Mary’s Syrian Roman Catholic, while the Arabic papers say Our Lady of Lebanon, so that detail is still open. Source: Brooklyn Times Union, 15 September 1932, page 22 (taken from the file name of the saved copy; the clipping itself does not print the paper or date). Names as printed: Joseph K. Owen, Affin, John, Mitchell, Louis, Anthony, Matilda, Theresa.

t: Document 70: John's court case over his birthday, 5 December 1940
x: John's court case over his birthday, 5 December 1940. Headed "Would Deny Birth Date Change To Man as 'Plan to Avoid Draft.'" The Eagle reports that a Syrian in Brooklyn Federal Court asked to change his birth date from 15 August 1905 to 15 August 1903, and that Assistant Federal Attorney Frank Parker opposed it on the ground that its only conceivable purpose was to avoid the draft. Judge Marcus B. Campbell reserved decision. The applicant is named as John Joseph Awn, a merchant of 1047 75th St., who immigrated on 5 September 1920 with his father, mother, two sisters and four brothers. His lawyer argued that 15 August 1905 could not be his birth date because it was his sister Theresa's. The case arose from the declaration of intention he filed that January. The judge's decision has not been found, and John's later papers give 4 August 1903 ( Confirmed as reported; the decision is Unknown). Source: Brooklyn Eagle, Thursday, 5 December 1940, p. 11, Brooklyn Newsstand (Newspapers.com), view source . Name as written: John Joseph Awn.
